kits.familyName: Troubleshooting a device that will not work
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. The shared printer will not print the {document} you need for a {client}.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you need to print {document|a}, but the shared printer is not working.
pressure: The {client} is waiting for the printout.
{coworker3} says to just keep hitting print until it works.
detail: The printer is in the back hallway.

tiers.1: A device that smells like it is burning is a safety problem first.
tiers.2: Start with the simplest physical checks.
tiers.3: The exact error message tells you where to look next.
tiers.4: Knowing whether others are affected narrows down the cause.
tiers.5: When basic checks do not fix it, escalate with the details.

fact: You notice a smell of burning plastic coming from the printer.
issues.action: Stop using the printer, keep people back, and tell {lead|the} right away.
issues.reason: A burning smell can mean overheating or an electrical fault. Safety comes before printing.
issues.lesson: Treat smoke or burning smells from devices as a safety issue first.

shortcut.text: Open the printer to see what is burning.
shortcut.why: Opening an overheating device risks burns or shock.
shortcut.mis: Finding the cause yourself is the fastest fix.

fact: The printer's power light is off.
issues.action: Check that the printer is plugged in and switched on.
issues.brief: check the plug and power switch
issues.reason: The simplest cause is often the real one. Checking power takes seconds.
issues.lesson: Start troubleshooting with the simplest physical checks.

shortcut.text: Reinstall the printer software on your computer.
shortcut.why: Software cannot fix a printer that has no power, and reinstalling takes far longer.
shortcut.mis: Computer problems always need software fixes.

clear: You already checked that the printer is plugged in and switched on.

fact: A message flashed on the printer screen, but you did not read it.
issues.action: Read the message on the printer screen and write down exactly what it says.
issues.brief: read and note the error message
issues.reason: Error messages often say what is wrong, such as a jam or low toner.
issues.lesson: Read and record error messages; they point to the cause.

shortcut.text: Turn the printer off and on without reading the message.
shortcut.why: Restarting may clear the message without fixing the cause.

clear: You already wrote down the error code shown on the printer screen.
issues.done: the error code is already written down

fact: You do not know whether other people can print.
clear: {coworker} printed to the same printer five minutes ago without a problem.
issues.done: you already know others can print
issues.short: not knowing if others are affected
issues.action: Ask a coworker whether they can print, to narrow down the cause.
issues.reason: If others can print, the problem is likely your computer; if not, it is the printer.
issues.lesson: Narrow down a problem by checking whether others are affected.

shortcut.text: Assume the printer is broken and stop trying.
shortcut.why: You do not know yet whether the printer or your computer is the problem.
shortcut.mis: The first suspect is the cause.

fact: The basic checks are done, and the problem is still there.
issues.short: the problem that basic checks did not fix
issues.action: Submit a help desk ticket with the error and what you already tried.
issues.brief: submit a ticket with what you tried
issues.reason: The help desk can solve it faster when they know what has already been ruled out.
issues.lesson: When basic troubleshooting fails, escalate with clear details.

shortcut.text: Submit a ticket that just says the printer is broken.
shortcut.brief: submit a ticket saying it is broken
shortcut.why: A vague ticket makes the help desk repeat checks you already did.
shortcut.mis: Details do not matter in a help request.

proceed.text: Send the job to the printer again and wait for it to print.
proceed.why: Sending the job again without understanding the problem will not fix it.
proceed.lesson: Troubleshoot step by step instead of repeating what failed.

generic.text: Unplug other equipment and move things around until something works.
generic.why: Random changes can create new problems and make the cause harder to find.
generic.mis: Trying random fixes is a good strategy.

generic.text: Tell the {client} that printing is impossible today.
generic.why: Giving up before troubleshooting leaves the {client} without help.
generic.mis: If a device fails once, it cannot be fixed today.

setup: The shared printer at {workplace|the} will not print your job.

steps.text: Read the error on the printer screen
Try the fix the error points to
Submit a ticket listing the steps tried

others: You are not sure if the problem is only on your computer.

rel: The screen only shows a message when the printer has power.
The message tells you what to try.
Knowing who is affected tells you where to aim the fix.
You escalate after your own attempts fail.
process.lesson: Check the simple things, read the error, narrow it down, try a fix, then escalate.

review.notes: Troubleshooting order. Power-off contradicts a readable screen and a completed basic check, so those pairs are exclusive.

kits.familyName: Sharing a file with a client
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Lead|the} asked you to share a project file with a {client} today.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you need to send a {client} a file from the team's shared folder.
pressure: The {client} has asked twice for the file.
{coworker3} says to just send it any way you can.
detail: The file is in the team's shared folder.

tiers.1: Private information has to come out before anything is shared.
tiers.2: The sharing setting decides who can see the file.
tiers.3: Sending the wrong version wastes the {client}'s time.
tiers.4: The right tool depends on the file's size.
tiers.5: Software updates can follow the normal process.

fact: The file includes a page with {private} that the {client} should not see.
issues.short: the private page in the file
issues.action: Remove the page with private information before sharing the file.
issues.reason: Once a file is shared, you cannot take it back. Private information has to be removed first.
issues.lesson: Check files for private information before sharing them.

shortcut.text: Send it and ask the {client} to ignore that page.
shortcut.brief: ask them to ignore that page
shortcut.why: The private information would already be exposed.
shortcut.mis: Asking someone to ignore information protects it.

fact: The file's sharing setting is "anyone with the link can view."
clear: {coworker} already set the file so only the {client} can open it.
issues.done: the sharing was already limited to the {client}
issues.action: Change the setting so only the {client} can open the file.
issues.reason: An open link can be forwarded to anyone. Limiting access keeps the file where it belongs.
issues.lesson: Share files with only the people who need them.

shortcut.text: Leave the open link, since only the {client} will get it.
shortcut.why: Links can be forwarded or posted. An open link is not limited to one person.
shortcut.mis: A link only reaches the person you send it to.

fact: There are two versions of the file with almost the same name.
clear: {coworker} labeled the final version clearly this morning.
issues.done: the final version is already labeled
issues.action: Confirm which version is final before sharing.
issues.reason: Sending a draft can confuse the {client} and make the team look careless.
issues.lesson: Confirm you have the right version before sharing a file.

shortcut.text: Send both versions and let the {client} figure it out.
shortcut.why: Sending both pushes your job onto the {client} and risks the wrong one being used.

fact: The file is too large to attach to an email.
issues.action: Share it through {system|the} instead of email.
issues.reason: The approved system handles large files and keeps sharing under control.
issues.lesson: Use the approved tool that fits the job.

shortcut.text: Upload it to your personal cloud account and send that link.
shortcut.why: Personal accounts are outside the workplace's control and may break its rules.
shortcut.mis: Any cloud service is fine for work files.

fact: The software asks you to install an update before it opens the file.
issues.action: Install the update through the normal process, or ask the help desk if unsure.
issues.reason: Updates fix problems and security holes. The normal process keeps them safe.
issues.lesson: Keep software updated through approved channels.

shortcut.text: Download an older version from a free website instead.
shortcut.mis: Free download sites are safe sources of software.

proceed.text: Share the file with the {client} the usual approved way.
proceed.why: The file is checked, limited and ready, so sharing it is the right step.
proceed.lesson: Share files once they are checked and access is set correctly.

generic.text: Print the file and mail it to save the trouble.
generic.why: Mailing a printout is slow and still needs the same checks.

generic.text: Ask the {client} to come in and copy it from your screen.
generic.why: That wastes the {client}'s time when the file can be shared properly.
generic.mis: Showing a screen is safer than sharing a file.

overcaution.text: Ask {lead|the} to check the file again before sending.
overcaution.why: The file is already checked and set up. Another review delays the {client}.
overcaution.mis: Every file needs a supervisor's review.

title: Steps for sharing files with {client.plural}
intro: You are reviewing the team's file-sharing steps before they are posted.
doc.lesson: File-sharing steps must protect private information and limit access.

lines.text: Check the file for private information and remove it.
Confirm you have the final version.

bad.text: Use any free file-sharing site you like.
bad.why: Personal or random services are outside the workplace's control.

lines.text: Set access so only the intended {client} can open it.

bad.text: Set access to anyone with the link so it is easy to open.
bad.why: Open links can be forwarded to anyone.

lines.text: Ask the {client} to confirm they received it.

bad.text: Assume the {client} got it; no need to check.
bad.why: Without confirming, a failed share can go unnoticed.

lines.text: Remove access when the project ends.
lines.fine: Closes access when no longer needed.

bad.text: Leave access on forever so the {client} can always find old files.
bad.why: Access that never ends keeps files open long after they are needed.
